follow_ups: Ask for the definition of a scan, the model and deployment architecture, unique validated vulnerabilities, time to remediation and changes in incident severity; scan volume alone does not measure security improvement.

Check patch testing, staged rollout and rollback practices, and measure change-induced outages alongside security gains. The episode does not establish that AI patching caused any specific external outage.
Track whether the public-private software-security proposal gains named participants, funding, supplier-access rules, liability arrangements and measurable remediation milestones.

Compare incremental client coverage and cost-to-serve with realized AI savings. Goldman's [2025 annual report](https://www.goldmansachs.com/investor-relations/financials/current/annual-reports/2025-annual-report) already describes One Goldman Sachs 3.0 and reinvestment of productivity gains; this interview clarifies the intended client segments, rather than announcing that programme.

signals.claim: Solomon says Goldman runs thousands to tens of thousands of daily AI-assisted vulnerability scans, while warning that rapid patching can destabilize systems.
signals.evidence: He says Goldman has had access to powerful models for seven to eight months and scans continuously to find and patch vulnerabilities. He judges the firm more secure than seven months earlier, while acknowledging remaining vulnerabilities. His broader explanation is that faster scanning and patching can create instability when changes are mishandled. The scan count is a first-party activity claim, not a count of distinct vulnerabilities fixed; he supplies no quantified outcome comparison or evidence establishing the cause of the Microsoft and FAA disruptions discussed by the hosts.

signals.claim: Solomon identifies weaker software suppliers as a security bottleneck and calls for public-private support to scan and patch the wider ecosystem.
signals.evidence: Discussing third-party software access, he says businesses need tighter information access, boundaries and vendor expectations. He says ordinary companies lack a large financial institution's resources and expertise, so he wants incentives and resources to extend scanning and remediation downstream. He says he is discussing a broad legacy-software upgrade effort with CEOs and government officials, and expects it to be costly and slow. This is a proposed coordination effort; he announces no funded programme, implementation commitments or coverage targets.

signals.claim: Solomon expects AI efficiencies to expand Goldman's institutional and ultra-high-net-worth coverage while preserving its direct-client focus.
signals.evidence: Asked whether AI lets Goldman move downmarket, he says he does not expect its institutional and ultra-high-net-worth focus to change materially over five to ten years. Goldman already distributes asset-management products to ordinary investors through other firms, without a direct relationship. He describes reinvesting process-efficiency margins in reaching more wealthy clients, institutions and growing businesses, rather than treating all savings as higher profit. He gives no savings amount, client-acquisition target or measured AI return; the contribution here is a segment-level clarification of an existing efficiency-and-growth strategy.

summary: Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon gives a concrete account of AI-assisted cyber defense: access to powerful models for seven to eight months and thousands to tens of thousands of vulnerability scans each day. He says the firm is more secure, while warning that rapid patching can itself disrupt systems. He also identifies less-resourced vendors' security capabilities as a weak point and proposes a public-private effort to upgrade legacy software. On commercial strategy, he expects technology efficiencies to support broader institutional and ultra-high-net-worth client coverage over five to ten years. These are operating claims and intentions, without quantified security outcomes or AI savings.
why_it_matters: The useful evidence is an incumbent's reported deployment scale and the constraints around it: discovering vulnerabilities is only part of the job; safe patch rollout and weaker suppliers also matter. Solomon's client-segment boundary clarifies where Goldman expects AI-enabled capacity to go. Track remediation outcomes, operational incidents and incremental client coverage to distinguish activity from economic benefit.
